title: 1948 Los Gatos DC-3 crash

location.name: Diablo Range near Los Gatos Creek

summary: On January 28, 1948, a Douglas DC-3 carrying 32 people including 28 Mexican nationals being deported crashed in the Diablo Range near Coalinga, California. A fuel leak in the port engine ignited, and the resulting fire burned through the wing spar until the port wing separated in flight. The aircraft spiraled to the ground in flames, killing all occupants.
probable_cause: Fuel leak in the port engine fuel pump ignited; the resulting fire burned through the wing structure, causing structural failure and loss of control.

title: BSAA Star Tiger disappearance
summary: BSAA Star Tiger, an Avro Tudor IV aircraft, disappeared without trace over the Atlantic Ocean on 30 January 1948 while en route from Santa Maria in the Azores to Bermuda. The aircraft was in radio contact until approximately 03:15 UTC when radio contact was lost. The investigation found want of care and attention to detail in the flight plan and noted the altitude chosen was much lower than usual. All 31 persons aboard disappeared.
probable_cause: The cause of the disappearance remains unknown. The official investigation found no evidence of radio failure, navigation error, or engine failure sufficient to explain the loss. The investigation found want of care and attention to detail in the flight plan but nothing serious enough to explain the accident.

title: Northwest Airlines 4422
summary: Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 4422, a C-54 charter from Shanghai, departed Anchorage but instead of following the published airway that detoured around Mount Sanford, the crew flew a direct line course. The aircraft was 23 miles off course and in dark night conditions struck Mount Sanford, Alaska. The wreckage slid approximately 3,000 feet down the mountain with no survivors.
probable_cause: The probable cause was navigation error with the aircraft flying off the published airway combined with dark night conditions preventing visual detection of the mountain.

title: 1948 Gatow air disaster
summary: A BEA Vickers Viking airliner on approach to RAF Gatow in West Berlin was struck by a Soviet Yakovlev Yak-3 fighter aircraft. The Soviet fighter was conducting aerobatic maneuvers in the vicinity of Gatow and had not coordinated with air traffic control. As the Viking made a left-hand turn on approach, the Yak-3 dived beneath it and pulled up sharply, clipping the Viking's port wing with its starboard wing. Both aircraft crashed; all occupants of both aircraft were killed. The incident occurred during escalating Cold War tensions over Berlin.
probable_cause: Midair collision caused by Soviet fighter aircraft conducting uncoordinated aerobatics in controlled airspace. The Yak-3 pilot was not under ATC control and failed to avoid the Viking on approach. Soviet aircraft were buzzing American and British passenger aircraft during this period of heightened tensions.

title: Pan Am 1-10
summary: Pan Am Flight 1-10, a Lockheed Constellation en route from London to Shannon, continued an instrument approach below safe altitude to clear terrain. A stone fence was struck 725 meters short of Runway 23. The pilot's instrument light had failed at earlier stops but could not be repaired due to lack of spare parts. The aircraft struck the fence while perfectly aligned with the runway but at an altitude insufficient to clear the obstacle.
probable_cause: The probable cause was continuation of an instrument approach to an altitude insufficient to clear the terrain. A contributing factor was failure of the pilot's instrument fluorescent light which had been inoperative since London.

title: 1948 Sabena DC-4 Crash
summary: A Sabena Douglas DC-4 was flying over the rainforest in Belgian Congo when it encountered severe weather at low altitude. The aircraft probably penetrated a very turbulent line of clouds or the active center of a tornado at 700 feet altitude. It was forced downward by a downward gust and hit the tree-tops, leaving a 200-meter trail through the forest before final impact. Only one survivor was recovered.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the aircraft penetrating a very turbulent line of clouds or flying into the active center of a tornado at low altitude (700 ft), which forced the aircraft to the ground by a downward gust.

title: United Airlines 624
summary: United Airlines Flight 624, a Douglas DC-6, experienced an erroneous fire warning in the cockpit and the crew deployed the fire extinguisher system containing CO2 gas. The crew activated the system without first manually operating the pressure relief valves as required by procedure, causing CO2 to escape into the cabin and cockpit. The crew became incapacitated by the gas concentration and the aircraft crashed into a hillside near Mount Carmel, Pennsylvania. Post-accident investigation found no evidence of actual fire.
probable_cause: Incapacitation of the crew by excessive CO2 gas concentration in the cockpit following deployment of the fire extinguisher system without opening required pressure relief valves.

title: 1948 Air France Latécoère 631 disappearance
summary: Air France Flight 072, a Latécoère 631 carrying 12 crew and 40 passengers, disappeared over the Atlantic Ocean on 1 August 1948. The aircraft departed Fort-de-France on 31 July at 14:50 GMT, due to arrive at Port-Etienne at 01:00 GMT on 1 August. A mayday distress signal was reportedly received just after midnight. Wreckage with evidence of fire was found 1570 nautical miles east of Puerto Rico. The aircraft was subsequently withdrawn from service.

factors.evidence: On 1 August 1948, Air France Flight 072 went missing over the Atlantic Ocean, presumably killing all 52 people on board.
Some of the wreckage showed evidence of fire.
Following the accident, which was the worst crash in the Atlantic Ocean at the time, the type was withdrawn from service by Air France.

events.text: The aircraft departed from Fort de France, Martinique at 14:50 GMT on 31 July, and was due to arrive at Port-Etienne, French West Africa at 01:00 GMT on 1 August.

USCGC Campbell reported finding two seats from the aircraft at a position 1570 nmi east of Puerto Rico, and some of the wreckage showed evidence of fire.

notes: Aircraft missing; cause never determined. Wreckage with fire evidence found.

title: Northwest Airlines 421
summary: Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 421, a Martin 2-0-2, crashed near Winona, Minnesota during descent on 29 August 1948. The aircraft's left wing separated in flight due to fatigue cracks in the wing root fittings. A wind gust in the thunderstorm encountered during descent triggered the failure. All 37 aboard were killed. The investigation revealed similar cracks on other Martin 2-0-2 aircraft and recommended increased inspection intervals and lower operating speeds.
probable_cause: The outer portion of the left wing separated due to fatigue cracks in the wing root fittings. The separation was triggered by either a wind gust in excess of design operating velocity, or a similar gust after the material had become fatigued. The investigation revealed fatigue cracks in similar locations on other Martin 2-0-2 aircraft.

title: Manono-Elizabethville flight crash
summary: A Sabena Douglas C-47A-10-DK aircraft on a scheduled passenger flight from Costermans City via Manono to Élizabethville crashed on August 31, 1948, near Kimbwe in the Belgian Congo. The aircraft went missing after taking off from Manono, and rescue operations found that the aircraft had made an emergency landing. All 13 people on board, including 3 crew members, were killed during the emergency landing. The exact cause of the crash remains undetermined despite favorable weather conditions at the time.

title: Bukken Bruse disaster
summary: The Short Sandringham flying boat crashed during water landing near Trondheim on October 2, 1948, killing 19 of 45 people aboard. Poor weather and foaming white seas created hazardous landing conditions. A wind gust struck the aircraft as it touched down, causing the pilots to lose control; the right wing float broke off and the aircraft rolled into the water with its nose ploughing into the bay.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by the pilot's loss of control during the attempt to land the Sandringham in a crosswind and rough seas with limited space available.

title: 1948 KLM Constellation air disaster
summary: A KLM Constellation on approach to Prestwick, Scotland became disoriented in deteriorating weather conditions after the crew relied on erroneous charts and an incomplete weather forecast. The pilot believed the cloud base was higher than it actually was and attempted an approach to runway 26. The aircraft struck electricity cables and crashed into high ground five miles east-northeast of the airport, killing all 40 aboard.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by the crew's reliance on erroneous charts and incomplete weather forecasts, causing the crew to become disoriented in inclement conditions.

factors.evidence: The crew relied on erroneous charts and became disoriented.
Prestwick was under drizzle with a cloud-base that was almost solid at 600 ft, with actual conditions as low as 300 ft in some areas.
The crew believed the cloud base was substantially higher and expected to have visual contact with the ground.
The aircraft crashed into high ground five miles east-northeast of the airfield after striking electricity cables.

events.text: Aircraft departed Amsterdam at 21:11 CET with 40 aboard for New York via Prestwick.

Pilot overflew runway 26, climbed to 450 ft, extended landing gear, then ran into what he believed was isolated cloud.
Aircraft struck electricity cables at 450 ft then crashed into high ground five miles east-northeast of airfield.

title: 1948 Airborne Transport DC-3 (DST) disappearance
summary: Captain Linquist reported landing gear warning light not functioning; batteries discharged and low on water. Aircraft left San Juan with batteries charged only enough to satisfy two-way radio with tower. Weather was fine but wind moved from northwest to northeast. At 04:13 Linquist reported 50 mi south of Miami but aircraft had only 1 hour 20 minutes fuel remaining. Aircraft overweight 118 lb. The aircraft then disappeared; no wreckage ever found.
